title: Phantom Read
description: Identify phantom rows with a two-session InnoDB example and distinguish statement snapshots, repeatable reads, range locks, and capacity invariants.

questions.question_text: What observation defines a phantom in the repeated-predicate example?
options: An existing row's value changes between two reads within the same transaction
The qualifying row set changes within one transaction because another transaction commits an insertion, deletion, or update crossing the predicate
A transaction reads uncommitted data
A transaction's write is silently overwritten by another transaction
questions.explanation: An update can move an existing row into or out of the predicate, so phantoms are not limited to INSERT or DELETE statements.

questions.question_text: T1 first lists Tuesday booking IDs 1 and 2. T2 inserts Tuesday booking 3 and commits. Under the stated READ COMMITTED ordinary-read lab, why can T1 next return ID 3?
options: Because Bob's balance changed
Its second statement uses a fresh committed snapshot containing T2’s inserted matching row
Because T1's query had a syntax error the first time
Because Alice's row was updated to match the condition
questions.explanation: Both reads belong to T1, but READ COMMITTED obtains a new consistent snapshot for each ordinary statement.

questions.question_text: Which distinction best describes the worked nonrepeatable-read and phantom examples?
options: They are the same anomaly with different names
The first isolates a changed value for one identified row; the second isolates changed membership of a predicate’s result set
Non-repeatable read only applies to numeric columns; phantom read applies to text columns
Phantom read requires three or more transactions; non-repeatable read requires only two
questions.explanation: A predicate’s membership can change through insertion, deletion, or an update crossing its boundary. Some update observations can overlap labels, so state the exact query property.

questions.question_text: Why does locking only the existing rows returned by a query not by itself block every new matching insertion?
options: Row-level locking is too slow to matter
A future matching row may be inserted into a gap not protected by those existing-row locks
Row-level locking only works for UPDATE statements
Phantom reads never involve row locks of any kind
questions.explanation: Protecting against such insertion can require suitable range or predicate coordination. Stable snapshot visibility can separately keep a repeated result unchanged without blocking the insertion.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a 'reverse phantom' scenario?
options: T1's first query returns 3 rows; T2 deletes one of those matching rows and commits; T1's second identical query now returns only 2 rows
T1 reads the same row's balance twice and gets different values
T1 reads a value written by T2 before T2 commits
T1's write is overwritten by T2's write
questions.explanation: A phantom can occur via deletion just as easily as insertion — the matching row SET shrinks instead of growing, but it's the same underlying anomaly (set of matching rows changed due to a committed operation from another transaction).

questions.question_text: Among the standard named isolation levels, which level specifies phantom prevention as a minimum requirement rather than relying on stronger engine-specific REPEATABLE READ behavior?
options: READ UNCOMMITTED
READ COMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE
Phantom reads cannot be prevented by any isolation level
questions.explanation: The standard minimum at REPEATABLE READ can permit phantoms, while engines such as PostgreSQL and ordinary InnoDB snapshot reads can provide stronger repeatability. Prevention does not universally require one particular locking implementation.

questions.question_text: If T1 runs two genuinely DIFFERENT queries (different WHERE conditions) and gets different row sets, is this a phantom read?
options: Yes, any differing result between two queries is a phantom read
No — phantom read specifically requires the SAME query/condition to be run twice; differing results from genuinely different queries are expected and not an anomaly
Only if the queries touch the same table
Only if T1 is a read-only transaction
questions.explanation: The anomaly requires comparing two executions of the identical condition; if the conditions differ, differing results are simply expected behavior, not a concurrency anomaly.

questions.question_text: How can a phantom read manifest through an aggregate query rather than a row list?
options: It cannot — phantom reads only ever affect SELECT * queries
A repeated COUNT(*) WHERE balance > 1000 could return 1 the first time and 2 the second time, reflecting the same underlying row-set change even though no individual row list was compared
Aggregate queries are immune to all concurrency anomalies
Only SUM() queries can exhibit phantom reads
questions.explanation: The same root cause (a new matching row committed in between two query executions) can be observed through a changing aggregate count/sum just as easily as through a changing row list.

questions.question_text: What is the defining observation in a phantom read?
options: A repeated predicate query sees changed qualifying membership
A password becomes visible
An index is rebuilt
A primary key is renamed
questions.explanation: Phantoms concern the set of rows satisfying a predicate.

questions.question_text: Must the competing change be uncommitted for a phantom?
options: Yes, every phantom is a dirty read
No, a committed insertion can cause it
Only if the row has a foreign key
Yes, COMMIT prevents all phantoms
questions.explanation: A phantom can occur entirely through committed changes.

questions.question_text: At InnoDB READ COMMITTED, when do ordinary consistent reads obtain snapshots?
options: Only at server startup
Each statement obtains a fresh snapshot
Only after ROLLBACK
All sessions share one permanent snapshot
questions.explanation: Fresh statement snapshots can expose newly committed qualifying rows.

questions.question_text: Why include both reads inside one transaction when demonstrating phantoms?
options: ORDER BY requires a transaction
Autocommit forbids SELECT
The repeatability property is being tested within that transaction
Rows cannot be inserted otherwise
questions.explanation: Comparing separate transactions does not test within-transaction repeatability.

questions.question_text: Does ORDER BY prevent phantom rows?
options: Yes, it locks every possible insertion
Only when ordering by an integer
Yes, if there are two rows
No, it only makes output order deterministic
questions.explanation: Ordering and predicate visibility are different concerns.

questions.question_text: A stable snapshot shows two rows while a new connection sees three. What follows?
options: The snapshot may hide a committed new row
The insertion certainly never committed
The server lost data
The table must be empty
questions.explanation: Snapshot stability does not imply that the competing insertion was blocked.

questions.question_text: Which update can create a phantom for price < 100?
options: Changing an unrelated label outside the result
Changing another row from price 120 to 90
Changing 120 to 130 outside the result
Updating a separate table only
questions.explanation: The update moves a row into the predicate set.

questions.question_text: Why are absent matching rows relevant to locking analysis?
options: Absence always locks the whole table
No-row results automatically serialize all writes
There may be no existing row to lock despite a set invariant
An empty result disables transactions
questions.explanation: A predicate can depend on future insertions into an otherwise empty range.

questions.question_text: Does a unique booking identifier enforce maximum bookings per day?
options: Yes, uniqueness limits every day to one row
Only for odd identifiers
Yes, when SELECT uses ORDER BY
No, distinct identifiers can still exceed daily capacity
questions.explanation: An identifier uniqueness constraint is different from aggregate capacity.

questions.question_text: Which InnoDB mechanism can protect ranges at REPEATABLE READ?
options: Next-key locking for suitable locking searches
ORDER BY alone
A display caption
A nonlocking snapshot alone
questions.explanation: Next-key locks can cover records and gaps for range protection.

questions.question_text: Why specify the engine with an isolation level?
options: Isolation names have no documented meaning
Implementations can provide different or stronger guarantees
All engines use identical snapshots
Only engine names determine SQL ordering
questions.explanation: The named level is not a complete cross-engine behavioral specification.

questions.question_text: Which additional observation distinguishes range blocking from snapshot invisibility?
options: Only the heading text
Only the query indentation
Whether the competing insert waited or committed
Only the number of table columns
questions.explanation: Both mechanisms can leave a reader displaying the old set, so writer behavior matters.

original_questions.question_text: What is the defining condition of a phantom read?
options: An existing row's value changes between two reads within the same transaction
The set of rows returned by the same query/condition, run twice within one transaction, differs because another transaction inserted or deleted a matching row in between
A transaction reads uncommitted data
A transaction's write is silently overwritten by another transaction
original_questions.explanation: Phantom read is specifically about the ROW SET matching a repeated query changing due to another transaction's committed insert/delete — not any existing row's value being updated.

original_questions.question_text: In the worked example, why does T1's second query return Carol's row when the first query didn't?
options: Because Bob's balance changed
Because T2 inserted a new row for Carol with balance 1500 and committed it in between T1's two identical query executions
Because T1's query had a syntax error the first time
Because Alice's row was updated to match the condition
original_questions.explanation: Carol's row didn't exist at the time of T1's first query; T2's committed insert created it in between, so it appears — as a 'phantom' — only in the second execution of the identical query.

original_questions.question_text: What is the precise distinction between a non-repeatable read and a phantom read?
options: They are the same anomaly with different names

Non-repeatable read: an EXISTING row's value changes between two reads. Phantom read: the SET of rows matching a condition changes because a new row was inserted (or an old one deleted), not because an existing row's value changed
Non-repeatable read only applies to numeric columns; phantom read applies to text columns
Phantom read requires three or more transactions; non-repeatable read requires only two
original_questions.explanation: This is the core distinguishing fact examiners test: non-repeatable read = same row, different value; phantom read = different set of rows entirely, via insert/delete.

original_questions.question_text: Why doesn't ordinary row-level locking (locking every row returned by a query) prevent phantom reads?
options: Row-level locking is too slow to matter

The phantom row does not exist yet at the time of the first query, so there is no row available to lock — preventing this requires locking the query's condition/range itself, not just already-returned rows
Row-level locking only works for UPDATE statements
Phantom reads never involve row locks of any kind
original_questions.explanation: Since the inserted row is brand new, no lock could have been placed on it before it existed; only a range/predicate lock on the condition itself can block new matching inserts.

original_questions.question_text: Which of the following is a 'reverse phantom' scenario?
options: T1's first query returns 3 rows; T2 deletes one of those matching rows and commits; T1's second identical query now returns only 2 rows
T1 reads the same row's balance twice and gets different values
T1 reads a value written by T2 before T2 commits
T1's write is overwritten by T2's write
original_questions.explanation: A phantom can occur via deletion just as easily as insertion — the matching row SET shrinks instead of growing, but it's the same underlying anomaly (set of matching rows changed due to a committed operation from another transaction).

original_questions.question_text: Which isolation level is typically required to fully prevent phantom reads?
options: READ UNCOMMITTED
READ COMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE (the strictest level, using range/predicate locking)
Phantom reads cannot be prevented by any isolation level
original_questions.explanation: Because preventing phantoms requires locking the query's predicate/range (not just existing rows), this guarantee is associated with the strongest, SERIALIZABLE isolation level.

original_questions.question_text: If T1 runs two genuinely DIFFERENT queries (different WHERE conditions) and gets different row sets, is this a phantom read?
options: Yes, any differing result between two queries is a phantom read
No — phantom read specifically requires the SAME query/condition to be run twice; differing results from genuinely different queries are expected and not an anomaly
Only if the queries touch the same table
Only if T1 is a read-only transaction
original_questions.explanation: The anomaly requires comparing two executions of the identical condition; if the conditions differ, differing results are simply expected behavior, not a concurrency anomaly.

options: It cannot — phantom reads only ever affect SELECT * queries
A repeated COUNT(*) WHERE balance > 1000 could return 1 the first time and 2 the second time, reflecting the same underlying row-set change even though no individual row list was compared
Aggregate queries are immune to all concurrency anomalies

original_questions.explanation: The same root cause (a new matching row committed in between two query executions) can be observed through a changing aggregate count/sum just as easily as through a changing row list.

notes:
## A changing set of matching rows

A phantom read occurs when a transaction repeats a predicate query and observes a changed set of qualifying rows because another transaction changed committed data between the reads. Imagine a coordinator listing all open laboratory bookings for Tuesday. The first query returns two bookings. Another session inserts a third Tuesday booking and commits. If the repeated query now includes the third row, the coordinator has observed a phantom. The important object is the predicate's result set, rather than only one previously identified row.

An insertion is the easiest example, but deletion or an update that moves a row into or out of the predicate can also change set membership. A query for price below 100 can gain a row when another transaction lowers a price from 120 to 90. A plain count can reveal the change without displaying the new row. For a clean teaching example, use an insertion so the difference from a changed value in an existing row remains obvious.

## Separate nearby anomalies

A dirty read consumes another transaction's uncommitted change. A phantom example can involve only committed data, so preventing dirty reads does not automatically prevent phantoms. A nonrepeatable read usually describes rereading an existing row and observing a changed value. A phantom concerns the membership of the set selected by a predicate. Some updates can be described in both ways depending on the observations being analyzed; state the query and the precise property instead of relying only on the label.

```text
Initial Tuesday bookings: ids 1 and 2
T1: SELECT ... WHERE booking_day = 'Tue'  → ids 1,2
T2: INSERT Tuesday booking id 3
T2: COMMIT
T1: SELECT ... WHERE booking_day = 'Tue'  → ids 1,2,3
```

The two T1 reads must belong to the transaction being studied. If each query is its own autocommit transaction, the changed result is ordinary observation across separate transactions, not a repeatability guarantee being tested within one transaction. Also distinguish a transaction's own insertions from another transaction's changes: seeing your own new row is normally expected and does not demonstrate an isolation failure. A useful test records both session boundaries and the writer responsible for each change.

## Reproduce the phenomenon under a specified level

The following example targets MySQL InnoDB READ COMMITTED with ordinary nonlocking SELECT statements. Set up the fixture before starting either session. The exact statements and order matter; changing the isolation level or adding a locking clause changes the experiment. Use two connections to a disposable learning database and coordinate the steps manually or through a test harness. This page describes expected behavior and does not claim that the exercise was executed here.

```sql
CREATE TABLE lab_booking (
  booking_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  booking_day VARCHAR(3) NOT NULL,
  INDEX booking_day_idx (booking_day)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
INSERT INTO lab_booking VALUES (1, 'Tue'), (2, 'Tue');

-- Session A
SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT booking_id FROM lab_booking
WHERE booking_day = 'Tue' ORDER BY booking_id;
-- Expected first output: 1, 2

-- Session B, after A's first read
INSERT INTO lab_booking VALUES (3, 'Tue');
-- With autocommit enabled, this statement commits itself.

-- Session A, after B's commit
SELECT booking_id FROM lab_booking
WHERE booking_day = 'Tue' ORDER BY booking_id;
-- Expected second output: 1, 2, 3
COMMIT;
```

InnoDB READ COMMITTED ordinary consistent reads take a fresh snapshot for each statement, allowing the second statement to see the newly committed row. The explicit ORDER BY makes the displayed comparison deterministic; it is not the mechanism that causes or prevents the phantom. If session B has not committed, session A's ordinary consistent read does not see B's uncommitted insertion. Coordinate the commit before comparing the second output to avoid drawing a conclusion from an incorrectly staged test.

## Snapshot stability and range protection

InnoDB REPEATABLE READ ordinarily uses a consistent snapshot established by the first consistent read in a transaction, unless an explicit consistent snapshot is established earlier. Repeating the ordinary snapshot query can therefore keep showing the original set even after B commits. This is visibility stability, not necessarily a reservation preventing other sessions from inserting. The new row can exist in committed storage while the older transaction continues to read its earlier snapshot.

Locking reads solve a different problem. Under InnoDB REPEATABLE READ, range searches can use next key locks, combining record and gap protection, to prevent competing insertions into the protected range. Index choice and search conditions determine which range is actually locked. A unique lookup of an existing unique key can have narrower locking than a range scan. Do not assume that adding FOR UPDATE to any query always locks exactly the conceptual business set and nothing else.

At READ COMMITTED, InnoDB generally disables gap locking for searches and index scans, with documented exceptions such as foreign key and duplicate key checks. Locking existing rows at that level does not generally reserve every place a future matching row could appear. This matters when the predicate currently matches zero rows. There may be no existing row to lock, yet the business decision still depends on the absence of future matches. Analyze absence and range protection explicitly.

## Stable reads do not prove every decision safe

Suppose two transactions each count Tuesday bookings and insert a different row if the count is below three. If both snapshots show two, both may insert, producing four bookings. A stable snapshot can hide a phantom from repeated reads while still allowing a problematic crossrow decision under the chosen protocol. Predicate visibility, write conflict detection, and serializable business behavior are related but distinct questions. Choose a mechanism that protects capacity, rather than merely making a report look stable.

Possible designs include serializing booking decisions on a shared laboratory day row, enforcing an appropriate slot representation with constraints, or using a documented serializable protocol with retry handling. Each choice requires analyzing the actual schema and workload. A uniqueness constraint on booking_id alone only prevents duplicate identifiers; it cannot enforce an aggregate capacity limit. Avoid treating an index as an automatic constraint on the number of rows satisfying an arbitrary predicate.

## Engine names are not interchangeable guarantees

The SQL isolation names describe minimum expected protections, while engines can provide stronger behavior. PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ, for example, prevents phantom reads through its snapshot implementation even though the standard's minimum for that level permits them. That does not make it identical to PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE for every anomaly. InnoDB ordinary consistent reads and locking reads also differ. State the engine, version family, isolation level, and statement type whenever predicting observable results.

Isolation tests should include the final committed set after both sessions end. That distinguishes a transaction's snapshot view from the current database state. Also record whether an insertion waited or an operation failed with a serialization or deadlock error. A blocked insertion and an invisible committed insertion can both make a reader display the original two rows, yet they reflect different coordination mechanisms. Looking only at the SELECT output can miss that essential distinction.

## Exercises with solutions

Exercise one: T1 counts two qualifying rows; T2 inserts one qualifying row and commits; T1 counts three. Classify the observation. It is a phantom within T1 if both counts belong to the same transaction and T2 caused the membership change. It is not a dirty read because T2 committed before the second read. If T1 had committed between counts, the example would instead compare two transactions.

Exercise two: T1's snapshot still shows two rows while a new connection sees three. Was B necessarily blocked? No. B may have committed successfully while T1 retained an older snapshot. Exercise three: a query locks two existing bookings at READ COMMITTED. Does that alone prove no third booking can be inserted? No. Existing row locks do not generally protect the entire future predicate range at that level. Compare [concurrent execution](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/concurrent-execution) and [transaction boundaries](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/transaction-boundaries) before designing a booking invariant test.


To extend the lab, reset the fixture and repeat it with an update that changes a Wednesday booking to Tuesday. Predict the first and second ordered result sets before running the sessions. Then repeat with a Tuesday deletion and explain which identifier disappears. These variants demonstrate that the predicate boundary, rather than the INSERT keyword, defines the phenomenon. Keep unrelated schema changes outside the experiment and finish every open transaction before changing session isolation settings. Save the observed statement order alongside the output so another reader can reproduce the same visibility question without relying on lucky timing.
